lines.text:
Caring for the Ones Who Cannot Speak — Inside a Vet Clinic

A veterinary clinic is a medical facility for animals — a place where diagnosis, treatment, surgery, and preventive care are performed on patients who cannot describe their symptoms. The veterinarian must read behaviour, physical signs, and test results to determine what is wrong. This makes veterinary medicine, in some ways, harder than human medicine.

The clinic is organised around patient flow. A waiting room separates species — dogs on one side, cats on the other, with smaller animals in carriers on laps or benches. A receptionist manages appointments, records, and payments. A pet owner checks in with a leash, a carrier, or a muzzle (for anxious animals). Treats help calm nervous patients.

The exam table is the clinical centre. A veterinarian (or vet) uses a stethoscope to listen to the heart and lungs. A thermometer takes temperature — rectally, in most animals. A scale records weight — essential for calculating medication doses. An otoscope examines the ears. More advanced diagnostics include an X-ray for bones and organs, an ultrasound for soft tissue, a blood test for organ function and infection, and a microscope for examining samples.

Common procedures span preventive and curative care. A vaccination protects against diseases. A microchip — a rice-grain-sized device injected under the skin — allows lost pets to be identified and returned. A spay (for females) and a neuter (for males) are surgical sterilisations. Dental cleaning removes plaque and tartar under anaesthesia. Medication — tablets, liquids, or injections — treats infections, pain, and chronic conditions. A syringe delivers injections. A bandage protects wounds. Stitches close surgical incisions. A cast immobilises broken bones. A cone collar — the plastic cone around the head — prevents the animal from licking or biting its wound.

The clinical spaces are specialised. An operating room is equipped for surgery. A lab processes blood, urine, and tissue samples. A pharmacy stocks medications. A recovery room allows animals to wake from anaesthesia under observation. A kennel houses animals that need overnight care. A grooming area provides bathing, brushing, and nail clipping. An outdoor run gives dogs exercise space.

The staff is multidisciplinary. A vet tech assists during examinations and procedures. A groomer handles hygiene. A kennel attendant feeds and monitors hospitalised animals. A surgeon performs complex operations. A specialist — in cardiology, oncology, or orthopaedics — handles referral cases. An intern learns under supervision. A volunteer supports non-clinical tasks.

Pet accessories are part of the vocabulary: a collar with a tag for identification, a leash for walking, a food bowl and a water dish for meals, nail clippers for grooming, and a brush for the coat.

Veterinary medicine requires scientific rigour and emotional intelligence in equal measure — because the patient cannot consent, cannot complain, and cannot understand why the treatment hurts. The vet's job is to heal the animal and to reassure the owner — simultaneously.

lines.text: ❌ "The vet gave us an advice about how to care for our rabbit after the surgery."
lines.name: ❌ "The vet gave us an advice about how to care for our rabbit after the surgery."

lines.text: ✅ "The vet gave us advice about how to care for our rabbit after the surgery."
lines.name: ✅ "The vet gave us advice about how to care for our rabbit after the surgery."

lines.text: 'Advice' is uncountable — never 'an advice' or 'advices.' Use: 'some advice', 'a piece of advice', 'the advice.' The verb form is 'advise' (different spelling and pronunciation): 'The vet advised us to...' Similar pairs: practice/practise (British), licence/license (British) — noun vs. verb.

lines.text: ❌ "The cat has been sick since three days and refuses to eat from its food bowl."
lines.name: ❌ "The cat has been sick since three days and refuses to eat from its food bowl."

lines.text: ✅ "The cat has been sick for three days and refuses to eat from its food bowl."
lines.name: ✅ "The cat has been sick for three days and refuses to eat from its food bowl."

lines.text: 'For' + duration: 'for three days', 'for a week.' 'Since' + point in time: 'since Monday', 'since the vaccination', 'since last night.' Never *'since three days' — three days is a duration, not a point in time. Present perfect + for/since: 'has been sick for three days' / 'has been sick since Tuesday.'

lines.text: ❌ "The veterinarian suggested us to bring the dog back for a follow-up examination."
lines.name: ❌ "The veterinarian suggested us to bring the dog back for a follow-up examination."

lines.text: ✅ "The veterinarian suggested that we bring the dog back for a follow-up examination."
lines.name: ✅ "The veterinarian suggested that we bring the dog back for a follow-up examination."

lines.text: 'Suggest' never takes object + infinitive (*suggest us to bring). Use: suggest + that-clause: 'suggested that we bring' (subjunctive). Suggest + gerund: 'suggested bringing the dog back.' Compare: 'The vet advised us to bring...' — 'advise' DOES take object + infinitive. Same restriction: 'recommend', 'propose.'

lines.text: ✅ "Each of the animals in the waiting room needs to be examined by the veterinarian."
lines.name: ✅ "Each of the animals in the waiting room needs to be examined by the veterinarian."

lines.text: 'Each' + singular verb: 'Each needs.' 'Each of the animals needs...' Compare: 'All of the animals need...' (plural). 'Every animal needs...' (singular). Don't be misled by the plural noun ('animals') between 'each of' and the verb — the subject is 'each', which is always singular.

lines.text: ❌ "The dog's health has been improved significantly since the surgery last month."
lines.name: ❌ "The dog's health has been improved significantly since the surgery last month."

lines.text: ✅ "The dog's health has improved significantly since the surgery last month."
lines.name: ✅ "The dog's health has improved significantly since the surgery last month."

lines.text: 'Improve' can be intransitive (no passive needed): 'Health has improved.' Using passive (*has been improved) implies an external agent actively improved it — possible but unusual for health. Intransitive: 'The condition has improved.' Transitive/passive: 'The treatment has been improved by researchers.' Choose active when the subject changes on its own.

lines.text: The UK is famous for being a nation of animal lovers. About 12 million households own a pet. Dogs and cats are the most popular, followed by rabbits, birds, and fish. The RSPCA (Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) is a major charity that rescues and rehomes animals.

lines.text: Vet care in the UK and US is expensive. A routine check-up costs £30-60. Surgery can cost £1,000+. Many pet owners buy pet insurance to cover unexpected vet bills. The PDSA (People's Dispensary for Sick Animals) provides free vet care for owners who can't afford it.

lines.text: He, She, or It for Animals?
lines.name: He, She, or It for Animals?

lines.text: Pets with a known sex: owners use 'he' or 'she'. Animals whose sex is unknown or unimportant: 'it'. In formal/scientific writing, 'it' is standard for all animals. 'They' (singular) is increasingly used when the sex is unknown: 'If a dog escapes, they might...'

lines.text: Put Down vs Put to Sleep
lines.name: Put Down vs Put to Sleep

lines.text: Both mean euthanasia — ending an animal's life to prevent suffering. 'Put to sleep' is the gentler euphemism. 'Put down' is more direct. Vets say 'euthanise' (formal). These are sensitive topics — use them carefully. Children may not understand euphemisms, so adults sometimes explain directly.
